expectedText:
LABOR OR SERVICES CONTRACTS WITHOUT FUNDS SUFFICIENT FOR LEGAL COMPLIANCE (LABOR CODE § 2810) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Builders, Inc.

ABOUT THIS LABOR CODE SECTION 2810 INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California Labor Code Section 2810, which addresses contracts for labor or services with construction, farm labor, garment, janitorial, security guard, port drayage motor carrier, and warehouse contractors that do not include enough money to let the contractor comply with the laws governing the work. Acme Builders, Inc. has described the labor or services contracts at issue as follows: Framing and drywall subcontracts on two residential projects. This document states the content of the statute and of a published California Court of Appeal decision construing it; it does not determine whether Section 2810 applies to any particular contract, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

THE CORE PROHIBITION: CONTRACTS WITHOUT FUNDS SUFFICIENT FOR LEGAL COMPLIANCE
Labor Code Section 2810 prohibits a person or entity from entering into a contract or agreement for labor or services with a construction, farm labor, garment, janitorial, security guard, port drayage motor carrier, or warehouse contractor when the person or entity knows or should know that the contract or agreement does not include funds sufficient to allow the contractor to comply with all applicable local, state, and federal laws or regulations governing the labor or services to be provided. The prohibition runs against the party that hires the contractor, and it operates at the moment the contract or agreement is entered into. A published Court of Appeal decision construing the section describes it as authorizing employees of a services contractor to sue the party that hired the contractor when that hiring party knowingly pays a contract price insufficient to permit compliance with the law in performing the contract.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "A person or entity shall not enter into a contract or agreement for labor or services with a construction, farm labor, garment, janitorial, security guard, port drayage motor carrier, or warehouse contractor, if the person or entity knows or should know that the contract or agreement does not include funds sufficient to allow the contractor to comply with all applicable local, state, and federal laws or regulations governing the labor or services to be provided."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, prohibition on underfunded labor or services contracts (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.)
  "section 2810 authorizes the employees of a services contractor to sue the party hiring the contractor if the hiring party knowingly pays a contract price insufficient to permit the contractor to comply with the law in performing the contract"
  — Castillo v. Toll Bros., Inc. (2011) 197 Cal.App.4th 1172, Court of Appeal description of what section 2810 authorizes (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810456/castillo-v-toll-bros-inc/)
  Known gap: The statute does not itself list which "applicable local, state, and federal laws or regulations" bear on a given contract, and it does not state a method for calculating whether a contract price is sufficient. The industries named in subdivision (a) are the only ones covered; a contract for labor or services outside those categories is not reached by this section. Section 2810 was most recently amended by Statutes 2024, Chapter 739 (AB 2754), effective January 1, 2025, whose Legislative Counsel's Digest states that the measure applied these provisions to port drayage motor carriers; decisions predating the current text construe a narrower list of covered contractors, and the 2011 Court of Appeal decision relied on elsewhere in this sheet quotes subdivision (a) as then reaching a "construction, farm labor, garment, janitorial, or security guard contractor."

WHO COUNTS AS A COVERED CONTRACTOR
Section 2810 defines the phrase describing covered contractors to include any person, as defined in the Labor Code, whether or not licensed, who is acting in the capacity of a construction, farm labor, garment, janitorial, security guard, port drayage motor carrier, or warehouse contractor. For this section, "warehouse" means a facility the primary operation of which is the storage or distribution of general merchandise, refrigerated goods, or other products, and "port drayage motor carrier" has the same meaning as in paragraph (5) of subdivision (a) of Labor Code Section 2810.4, which defines that term to mean an individual or entity that hires or engages commercial drivers in the port drayage industry, and which also reaches specified owners, lessees, licensees, or bailees of commercial motor vehicles and successor entities.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "The phrase “construction, farm labor, garment, janitorial, security guard, port drayage motor carrier, or warehouse contractor” includes any person, as defined in this code, whether or not licensed, who is acting in the capacity of a construction, farm labor, garment, janitorial, security guard, port drayage motor carrier, or warehouse contractor."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810(h) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, scope of the covered-contractor phrase (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.)
  "For the purposes of this section, “warehouse” means a facility the primary operation of which is the storage or distribution of general merchandise, refrigerated goods, or other products."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810(j) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, definition of "warehouse" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.)
  "For the purposes of this section, “port drayage motor carrier” has the same meaning as in paragraph (5) of subdivision (a) of Section 2810.4."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810(k) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, cross-reference for "port drayage motor carrier" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.)
  "“Port drayage motor carrier” means an individual or entity that hires or engages commercial drivers in the port drayage industry."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.4(a)(5)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, definition of "port drayage motor carrier" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.4.)
  Known gap: Because coverage turns on acting "in the capacity of" one of the listed contractor types rather than on holding a license, a contractor's lack of a license does not remove the contract from the section. The statute does not define "construction," "farm labor," "garment," "janitorial," or "security guard" contractor within this section, and the full definition of "port drayage motor carrier" appears in Section 2810.4, subdivision (a)(5), whose subparagraphs (B) and (C) add owner/lessee/licensee/bailee and successor coverage that is summarized rather than quoted here.

CONTRACTS THE PROHIBITION DOES NOT REACH
Subdivision (a) does not apply to three categories of contracting party or contract. It does not apply to a person or entity who executes a collective bargaining agreement covering the workers employed under the contract or agreement. It does not apply to a person who enters into a contract or agreement for labor or services to be performed on that person's home residences, provided that a family member resides in the residence or residences for which the labor or services are to be performed for at least a part of the year. And it does not apply to a contract with a port drayage motor carrier involving 30 days or fewer of cumulative labor or services within a one-year period.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "A person or entity who executes a collective bargaining agreement covering the workers employed under the contract or agreement."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, collective bargaining agreement exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.)
  "A person who enters into a contract or agreement for labor or services to be performed on that person’s home residences, provided that a family member resides in the residence or residences for which the labor or services are to be performed for at least a part of the year."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, home residence exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.)
  "A contract with a port drayage motor carrier involving 30 days or fewer of cumulative labor or services within a one-year period."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810(c)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, short-duration port drayage exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.)
  Known gap: The home-residence exception is written in terms of a natural person's "home residences" and a family-member residency requirement for at least part of the year; the statute does not define "family member" or state how the part-year residency is measured. The statute does not state who bears the burden of establishing that an exception applies, and whether a given arrangement fits one of these three exceptions is a fact-specific determination this sheet does not make.

THE REBUTTABLE PRESUMPTION FOR A COMPLETE WRITTEN CONTRACT
Section 2810 creates a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof that there has been no violation of subdivision (a) if the contract or agreement with a covered contractor meets all of the requirements in subdivision (d). To meet those requirements, the contract or agreement must be in writing, in a single document, and contain all of the provisions listed in subdivision (d), in addition to any other provisions the Labor Commissioner may require by regulation. The listed provisions include the parties' identifying information; a description of the labor or services and when they are to be commenced and completed; the contractor's state employer identification number; the contractor's workers' compensation policy number and carrier information; vehicle identification and liability insurance information for contractor-owned vehicles used in the work; the address of any real property used to house workers; the total number of workers, the total amount of all wages to be paid, and the dates those wages are to be paid; the amount of the commission or other payment to the contractor; information about persons used as independent contractors, including license or motor carrier authority numbers and copies of their agreements; and the signatures of all parties with the date of signing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "There is a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof that there has been no violation of subdivision (a) if the contract or agreement with a construction, farm labor, garment, janitorial, security guard, port drayage motor carrier, or warehouse contractor meets all of the requirements in subdivision (d)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, rebuttable presumption of no violation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.)
  "To meet the requirements of subdivision (b), a contract or agreement with a construction, farm labor, garment, janitorial, security guard, port drayage motor carrier, or warehouse contractor for labor or services shall be in writing, in a single document, and contain all of the following provisions, in addition to any other provisions that may be required by regulations adopted by the Labor Commissioner from time to time:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, single written document requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.)
  "The total number of workers to be employed under the contract or agreement, the total amount of all wages to be paid, and the date or dates when those wages are to be paid."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810(d)(7) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, required wage and workforce terms (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.)
  "The amount of the commission or other payment made to the construction, farm labor, garment, janitorial, security guard, port drayage motor carrier, or warehouse contractor for services under the contract or agreement."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810(d)(8) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, required statement of the contractor's payment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.)
  "The signatures of all parties, and the date the contract or agreement was signed."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810(d)(10) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, signature requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.)
  Known gap: The presumption described in subdivision (b) is a presumption affecting the burden of proof, not a safe harbor: the statute makes it rebuttable and does not say what evidence rebuts it. Paragraphs (1) through (6) and (9) of subdivision (d) are summarized rather than quoted in this clause; the complete list must be read in the statute. The statute also contemplates additional contract provisions "required by regulations adopted by the Labor Commissioner from time to time," and this sheet does not survey whether any such regulations exist.

MATERIAL CHANGES AND ESTIMATED FIGURES
To qualify for the rebuttable presumption, a material change to the terms and conditions of a contract or agreement between a person or entity and a covered contractor must be in writing, in a single document, and contain all of the provisions listed in subdivision (d) that are affected by the change. If a provision required by paragraph (7) (workers, total wages, and payment dates) or paragraph (9) (independent contractor information) of subdivision (d) is unknown when the contract is executed, the best estimate available at that time satisfies subdivision (d). Where an estimate is used in place of actual figures, the parties have a continuing duty to ascertain the required information and to reduce it to writing once that information becomes known.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "To qualify for the rebuttable presumption set forth in subdivision (b), a material change to the terms and conditions of a contract or agreement between a person or entity and a construction, farm labor, garment, janitorial, security guard, port drayage motor carrier, or warehouse contractor must be in writing, in a single document, and contain all of the provisions listed in subdivision (d) that are affected by the change."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810(e)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, writing requirement for material changes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.)
  "If a provision required to be contained in a contract or agreement pursuant to paragraph (7) or (9) of subdivision (d) is unknown at the time the contract or agreement is executed, the best estimate available at that time is sufficient to satisfy the requirements of subdivision (d). If an estimate is used in place of actual figures in accordance with this paragraph, the parties to the contract or agreement have a continuing duty to ascertain the information required pursuant to paragraph (7) or (9) of subdivision (d) and to reduce that information to writing in accordance with the requirements of paragraph (1) once that information becomes known."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810(e)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, best-estimate rule and continuing duty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.)
  Known gap: The statute does not define "material change," and it does not state a deadline for reducing newly known figures to writing beyond the requirement that the parties do so "once that information becomes known." The continuing duty described here is tied to the presumption in subdivision (b); the statute does not state a separate penalty for failing to update an estimate.

FOUR-YEAR RETENTION AND LABOR COMMISSIONER ACCESS
A person or entity who enters into a contract or agreement referred to in subdivisions (d) or (e) must keep a copy of the written contract or agreement for not less than four years following the termination of the contract or agreement. On the Labor Commissioner's request, the person or entity must provide the Labor Commissioner a copy of the provisions of the contract or agreement, and any other documentation, related to paragraphs (1) to (10), inclusive, of subdivision (d). Documents obtained by the Labor Commissioner under this section are exempt from disclosure under the California Public Records Act.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "A person or entity who enters into a contract or agreement referred to in subdivisions (d) or (e) shall keep a copy of the written contract or agreement for a period of not less than four years following the termination of the contract or agreement. Upon the request of the Labor Commissioner, any person or entity who enters into the contract or agreement shall provide to the Labor Commissioner a copy of the provisions of the contract or agreement, and any other documentation, related to paragraphs (1) to (10), inclusive, of subdivision (d)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810(f) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, four-year retention and production to the Labor Commissioner (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.)
  Known gap: The retention duty attaches to contracts "referred to in subdivisions (d) or (e)" — that is, the written contracts and written material changes used to qualify for the presumption — and the statute does not state a separate penalty within Section 2810 for failing to retain or produce them. The Public Records Act exemption is stated by cross-reference to Division 10 (commencing with Section 7920.000) of Title 1 of the Government Code, whose terms are not set out in this section.

EMPLOYEE ACTIONS, DAMAGES, AND THE INJURY REQUIREMENT
An employee aggrieved by a violation of subdivision (a) may file an action for damages to recover the greater of all of the employee's actual damages or $250 per employee per violation for an initial violation and $1,000 per employee for each subsequent violation, and, on prevailing, may recover costs and reasonable attorney's fees. Such an action may not be maintained unless it is pleaded and proved that an employee was injured as a result of a violation of a labor law or regulation in connection with the performance of the contract or agreement. An aggrieved employee may also bring an action for injunctive relief and, on prevailing, may recover costs and reasonable attorney's fees.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "An employee aggrieved by a violation of subdivision (a) may file an action for damages to recover the greater of all of the employee’s actual damages or two hundred fifty dollars ($250) per employee per violation for an initial violation and one thousand dollars ($1,000) per employee for each subsequent violation, and, upon prevailing in an action brought pursuant to this section, may recover costs and reasonable attorney’s fees."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810(g)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, damages, penalties, costs, and fees (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.)
  "An action under this section shall not be maintained unless it is pleaded and proved that an employee was injured as a result of a violation of a labor law or regulation in connection with the performance of the contract or agreement."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810(g)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, requirement to plead and prove injury (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.)
  "An employee aggrieved by a violation of subdivision (a) may also bring an action for injunctive relief and, upon prevailing, may recover costs and reasonable attorney’s fees."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810(g)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, injunctive relief (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.)
  Known gap: The statute gives the private right of action to an "employee aggrieved by a violation of subdivision (a)" and does not, in this section, state a limitations period, address class treatment, or address enforcement by the Labor Commissioner through a citation. The injury requirement is a pleading-and-proof requirement tied to a violation of a labor law or regulation in connection with performance of the contract, which means a defective contract alone is not described by the statute as supporting a damages action.

WHAT "KNOWS" AND "SHOULD KNOW" MEAN
Section 2810 defines the knowledge element in three parts. The term "knows" includes knowledge, arising from familiarity with the normal facts and circumstances of the business activity engaged in, that the contract or agreement does not include funds sufficient to allow the contractor to comply with applicable laws. The phrase "should know" includes knowledge of any additional facts or information that would make a reasonably prudent person undertake to inquire whether, taken together, the contract or agreement contains sufficient funds to allow the contractor to comply with applicable laws. A failure by a person or entity to request or obtain any information from the contractor that is required by any applicable statute or by the contract between them constitutes knowledge of that information for purposes of the section. Construing these provisions, the Court of Appeal stated that they charge a contracting party with knowledge typical in the industry as well as with knowledge of any additional facts or information reasonably suggesting insufficiency, and that because subdivision (a) precludes entering into an insufficient contract, the party's knowledge is determined at the time the contract is executed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "The term “knows” includes the knowledge, arising from familiarity with the normal facts and circumstances of the business activity engaged in, that the contract or agreement does not include funds sufficient to allow the contractor to comply with applicable laws."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810(i)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, definition of "knows" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.)
  "The phrase “should know” includes the knowledge of any additional facts or information that would make a reasonably prudent person undertake to inquire whether, taken together, the contract or agreement contains sufficient funds to allow the contractor to comply with applicable laws."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810(i)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, definition of "should know" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.)
  "A failure by a person or entity to request or obtain any information from the contractor that is required by any applicable statute or by the contract or agreement between them, constitutes knowledge of that information for purposes of this section."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810(i)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, failure to request required information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.)
  "Taken together, these two provisions charge a contracting party with knowledge typical in the industry, as well as with knowledge of any “additional facts or information” reasonably suggesting insufficiency."
  — Castillo v. Toll Bros., Inc. (2011) 197 Cal.App.4th 1172, Court of Appeal reading of the two statutory knowledge definitions (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810456/castillo-v-toll-bros-inc/)
  "Because subdivision (a) precludes a contracting party from entering into an insufficient contract, the party’s knowledge must be determined at the time the contract is executed."
  — Castillo v. Toll Bros., Inc. (2011) 197 Cal.App.4th 1172, Court of Appeal on the time at which knowledge is measured (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810456/castillo-v-toll-bros-inc/)
  Known gap: Each definition is phrased as what the term "includes," so the statutory text is not an exhaustive definition of actual or constructive knowledge. Castillo v. Toll Bros., Inc. is a decision of the First District Court of Appeal, and it construed the version of Section 2810 in effect before the 2024 amendment, when subdivision (a) reached a "construction, farm labor, garment, janitorial, or security guard contractor"; the knowledge definitions it construed appear at subdivision (i)(1) and (i)(2) in the current text as well. This sheet does not survey later decisions agreeing or disagreeing with Castillo.

THE TWO-PART SHOWING DESCRIBED IN CASTILLO V. TOLL BROS.
In Castillo v. Toll Bros., Inc., the First District Court of Appeal addressed wage-and-hour claims brought by subcontractors' employees against a homebuilder under Section 2810. The court described the determination called for by subdivision (a) as encompassing two separate questions for a complex contract: the contracting party's actual or constructive knowledge of insufficiency, which is prospective and evaluated when the contract is executed, and actual insufficiency, which is retrospective and can be determined only after the cost of performance is known. The court stated that a contracting party can be held liable under Section 2810 only if it knew or should have known the contract price was reasonably likely to be insufficient at the time the contract was executed and the contract price proved insufficient in practice. The court also rejected a narrower reading of "knows or should know" that would require genuine knowledge of insufficiency at signing, reasoning that such a definition would allow a contracting party to evade liability by cultivating ignorance in its contractual relations.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "A contracting party can be held liable under section 2810 only if (1) it knew or should have known the contract price was reasonably likely to be insufficient at the time the contract was executed and (2) the contract price proved insufficient in practice."
  — Castillo v. Toll Bros., Inc. (2011) 197 Cal.App.4th 1172, Court of Appeal statement of the two-part liability showing (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810456/castillo-v-toll-bros-inc/)
  "the determination called for by subdivision (a) encompasses two separate questions for a complex contract: the contracting party’s actual or constructive knowledge of insufficiency and actual insufficiency."
  — Castillo v. Toll Bros., Inc. (2011) 197 Cal.App.4th 1172, Court of Appeal framing of the two separate questions (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810456/castillo-v-toll-bros-inc/)
  "The first question, the contracting party’s knowledge, is necessarily a prospective determination, evaluated at the time the contract was executed."
  — Castillo v. Toll Bros., Inc. (2011) 197 Cal.App.4th 1172, Court of Appeal on the prospective and retrospective questions (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810456/castillo-v-toll-bros-inc/)
  "Whether a contract price was sufficient in fact can only be determined after the cost of performance, including the actual cost of materials and overhead and the actual amount and type of labor necessary, has been determined through the employer’s experience in performing the contract."
  — Castillo v. Toll Bros., Inc. (2011) 197 Cal.App.4th 1172, Court of Appeal on why actual insufficiency is retrospective (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810456/castillo-v-toll-bros-inc/)
  "Any such definition is unworkable, given the common difficulty in determining whether a particular contract is insufficient."
  — Castillo v. Toll Bros., Inc. (2011) 197 Cal.App.4th 1172, Court of Appeal rejecting an actual-knowledge-only reading (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810456/castillo-v-toll-bros-inc/)
  "Only in unusual circumstances will the insufficiency of a contract be so clear that a contracting party can be said to have actual knowledge of the insufficiency, particularly if the contracting party has made no attempt to determine the details of the employer’s proposed performance."
  — Castillo v. Toll Bros., Inc. (2011) 197 Cal.App.4th 1172, Court of Appeal on when actual knowledge of insufficiency will exist (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810456/castillo-v-toll-bros-inc/)
  Known gap: Castillo is a Court of Appeal decision, not a decision of the California Supreme Court, and it arose on review of summary judgment and summary adjudication rulings; the court affirmed in part and reversed in part, remanding the Section 2810 claim in one of the two consolidated matters. The opinion construed an earlier version of the statute, quoting subdivision (a) as then reaching a "construction, farm labor, garment, janitorial, or security guard contractor," and its two-question framing is expressly addressed to a "complex contract" whose labor and materials costs cannot be known with certainty at signing. The sentence quoted here describing the two separate questions is quoted from "the determination called for" onward and ends before a footnote-reference marker that immediately follows the word "insufficiency" in the source text; the court's further statement that a narrow actual-knowledge rule "would defeat the obvious purpose of section 2810, since it would allow a contracting party to evade liability ... by cultivating ignorance in its contractual relations" is interrupted mid-sentence by a star-pagination marker (*1198) in the available text, so the adjacent unbroken sentences are quoted instead.

THE WAGE STANDARD USED TO MEASURE SUFFICIENCY
Castillo v. Toll Bros., Inc. addressed which wage level is used to decide whether a contract includes sufficient funds. The plaintiffs argued that sufficiency should be measured against the locally prevailing wage for comparable work; the court held that the statutory language unambiguously requires the sufficiency of a contract challenged under Section 2810 to be measured by the minimum wage cost for the work anticipated. The court reasoned that there is no general law requiring an employer to pay its workers the average local wage for a particular skill or trade if that average wage is higher than the legal minimum, so paying less than the prevailing wage violates no law, and that Section 2810 imposes nothing more than compliance with legal requirements. The court used the term "minimum wage" to mean the minimum permissible wage under applicable state and local law for the work covered by the contract, noting that on some jobs, notably those requiring payment of the prevailing wage, the minimum permissible wage may be higher than the Industrial Welfare Commission's designated minimum wage.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "we conclude the statutory language unambiguously requires the sufficiency of a contract challenged under section 2810 to be measured by the minimum wage cost for the work anticipated"
  — Castillo v. Toll Bros., Inc. (2011) 197 Cal.App.4th 1172, Court of Appeal holding on the standard for measuring sufficiency (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810456/castillo-v-toll-bros-inc/)
  "Plaintiffs’ position is untenable because there is no general law requiring an employer to pay its workers the average local wage for a particular skill or trade, if that average wage is higher than the legal minimum."
  — Castillo v. Toll Bros., Inc. (2011) 197 Cal.App.4th 1172, Court of Appeal on the absence of a prevailing-wage requirement (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810456/castillo-v-toll-bros-inc/)
  "In this and the following parts, we use the term “minimum wage” to mean the minimum permissible wage under applicable state and local law for the work covered by the contract at issue."
  — Castillo v. Toll Bros., Inc. (2011) 197 Cal.App.4th 1172, Court of Appeal footnote defining "minimum wage" as used in the opinion (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810456/castillo-v-toll-bros-inc/)
  "On some jobs, notably those requiring payment of the prevailing wage, the minimum permissible wage may be higher than the commission’s designated minimum wage."
  — Castillo v. Toll Bros., Inc. (2011) 197 Cal.App.4th 1172, Court of Appeal footnote on jobs requiring the prevailing wage (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810456/castillo-v-toll-bros-inc/)
  Known gap: This clause reports how one published Court of Appeal decision construed the statute; the statutory text itself refers only to "funds sufficient to allow the contractor to comply with all applicable local, state, and federal laws or regulations" and names no wage standard. The court's own footnote makes clear that where a prevailing wage law does apply to the work, the prevailing wage can be the minimum permissible wage, so the holding is about the absence of a free-floating market-wage requirement rather than about public works; the last two quotations below come from that footnote rather than from the body of the opinion. The first quotation begins mid-sentence, after the introductory words "Based on these provisions," in the source. Sufficiency also depends on costs beyond wages, such as legally required payroll contributions, which this clause does not enumerate, and Castillo construed the statute as it read before the 2024 amendment.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
This information sheet regarding California Labor Code Section 2810 was prepared by Jordan T. Reyes for Acme Builders, Inc. and reviewed in Oakland, California on September 13, 2026. It reflects the statutory text and case law as of the date checked above and does not reflect any amendments or decisions issued after that date.

Acme Builders, Inc. has described the labor or services contracts at issue as follows: Framing and drywall subcontracts on two residential projects. This document states the content of the statute and of a published California Court of Appeal decision construing it; it does not determine whether Section 2810 applies to any particular contract, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

Labor Code Section 2810 prohibits a person or entity from entering into a contract or agreement for labor or services with a construction, farm labor, garment, janitorial, security guard, port drayage motor carrier, or warehouse contractor when the person or entity knows or should know that the contract or agreement does not include funds sufficient to allow the contractor to comply with all applicable local, state, and federal laws or regulations governing the labor or services to be provided. The prohibition runs against the party that hires the contractor, and it operates at the moment the contract or agreement is entered into. A published Court of Appeal decision construing the section describes it as authorizing employees of a services contractor to sue the party that hired the contractor when that hiring party knowingly pays a contract price insufficient to permit compliance with the law in performing the contract.

expectedJSON.gap: The statute does not itself list which "applicable local, state, and federal laws or regulations" bear on a given contract, and it does not state a method for calculating whether a contract price is sufficient. The industries named in subdivision (a) are the only ones covered; a contract for labor or services outside those categories is not reached by this section. Section 2810 was most recently amended by Statutes 2024, Chapter 739 (AB 2754), effective January 1, 2025, whose Legislative Counsel's Digest states that the measure applied these provisions to port drayage motor carriers; decisions predating the current text construe a narrower list of covered contractors, and the 2011 Court of Appeal decision relied on elsewhere in this sheet quotes subdivision (a) as then reaching a "construction, farm labor, garment, janitorial, or security guard contractor."

expectedJSON.body: Section 2810 defines the phrase describing covered contractors to include any person, as defined in the Labor Code, whether or not licensed, who is acting in the capacity of a construction, farm labor, garment, janitorial, security guard, port drayage motor carrier, or warehouse contractor. For this section, "warehouse" means a facility the primary operation of which is the storage or distribution of general merchandise, refrigerated goods, or other products, and "port drayage motor carrier" has the same meaning as in paragraph (5) of subdivision (a) of Labor Code Section 2810.4, which defines that term to mean an individual or entity that hires or engages commercial drivers in the port drayage industry, and which also reaches specified owners, lessees, licensees, or bailees of commercial motor vehicles and successor entities.

expectedJSON.gap: Because coverage turns on acting "in the capacity of" one of the listed contractor types rather than on holding a license, a contractor's lack of a license does not remove the contract from the section. The statute does not define "construction," "farm labor," "garment," "janitorial," or "security guard" contractor within this section, and the full definition of "port drayage motor carrier" appears in Section 2810.4, subdivision (a)(5), whose subparagraphs (B) and (C) add owner/lessee/licensee/bailee and successor coverage that is summarized rather than quoted here.

expectedJSON.body: Subdivision (a) does not apply to three categories of contracting party or contract. It does not apply to a person or entity who executes a collective bargaining agreement covering the workers employed under the contract or agreement. It does not apply to a person who enters into a contract or agreement for labor or services to be performed on that person's home residences, provided that a family member resides in the residence or residences for which the labor or services are to be performed for at least a part of the year. And it does not apply to a contract with a port drayage motor carrier involving 30 days or fewer of cumulative labor or services within a one-year period.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, collective bargaining agreement exception
citations.quote: A person or entity who executes a collective bargaining agreement covering the workers employed under the contract or agreement.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, home residence exception
citations.quote: A person who enters into a contract or agreement for labor or services to be performed on that person’s home residences, provided that a family member resides in the residence or residences for which the labor or services are to be performed for at least a part of the year.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810(c)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, short-duration port drayage exception
citations.quote: A contract with a port drayage motor carrier involving 30 days or fewer of cumulative labor or services within a one-year period.

expectedJSON.gap: The home-residence exception is written in terms of a natural person's "home residences" and a family-member residency requirement for at least part of the year; the statute does not define "family member" or state how the part-year residency is measured. The statute does not state who bears the burden of establishing that an exception applies, and whether a given arrangement fits one of these three exceptions is a fact-specific determination this sheet does not make.

expectedJSON.body: Section 2810 creates a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof that there has been no violation of subdivision (a) if the contract or agreement with a covered contractor meets all of the requirements in subdivision (d). To meet those requirements, the contract or agreement must be in writing, in a single document, and contain all of the provisions listed in subdivision (d), in addition to any other provisions the Labor Commissioner may require by regulation. The listed provisions include the parties' identifying information; a description of the labor or services and when they are to be commenced and completed; the contractor's state employer identification number; the contractor's workers' compensation policy number and carrier information; vehicle identification and liability insurance information for contractor-owned vehicles used in the work; the address of any real property used to house workers; the total number of workers, the total amount of all wages to be paid, and the dates those wages are to be paid; the amount of the commission or other payment to the contractor; information about persons used as independent contractors, including license or motor carrier authority numbers and copies of their agreements; and the signatures of all parties with the date of signing.

citations.quote: There is a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof that there has been no violation of subdivision (a) if the contract or agreement with a construction, farm labor, garment, janitorial, security guard, port drayage motor carrier, or warehouse contractor meets all of the requirements in subdivision (d).

citations.quote: To meet the requirements of subdivision (b), a contract or agreement with a construction, farm labor, garment, janitorial, security guard, port drayage motor carrier, or warehouse contractor for labor or services shall be in writing, in a single document, and contain all of the following provisions, in addition to any other provisions that may be required by regulations adopted by the Labor Commissioner from time to time:

expectedJSON.gap: The presumption described in subdivision (b) is a presumption affecting the burden of proof, not a safe harbor: the statute makes it rebuttable and does not say what evidence rebuts it. Paragraphs (1) through (6) and (9) of subdivision (d) are summarized rather than quoted in this clause; the complete list must be read in the statute. The statute also contemplates additional contract provisions "required by regulations adopted by the Labor Commissioner from time to time," and this sheet does not survey whether any such regulations exist.

expectedJSON.body: To qualify for the rebuttable presumption, a material change to the terms and conditions of a contract or agreement between a person or entity and a covered contractor must be in writing, in a single document, and contain all of the provisions listed in subdivision (d) that are affected by the change. If a provision required by paragraph (7) (workers, total wages, and payment dates) or paragraph (9) (independent contractor information) of subdivision (d) is unknown when the contract is executed, the best estimate available at that time satisfies subdivision (d). Where an estimate is used in place of actual figures, the parties have a continuing duty to ascertain the required information and to reduce it to writing once that information becomes known.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810(e)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, writing requirement for material changes
citations.quote: To qualify for the rebuttable presumption set forth in subdivision (b), a material change to the terms and conditions of a contract or agreement between a person or entity and a construction, farm labor, garment, janitorial, security guard, port drayage motor carrier, or warehouse contractor must be in writing, in a single document, and contain all of the provisions listed in subdivision (d) that are affected by the change.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810(e)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, best-estimate rule and continuing duty
citations.quote: If a provision required to be contained in a contract or agreement pursuant to paragraph (7) or (9) of subdivision (d) is unknown at the time the contract or agreement is executed, the best estimate available at that time is sufficient to satisfy the requirements of subdivision (d). If an estimate is used in place of actual figures in accordance with this paragraph, the parties to the contract or agreement have a continuing duty to ascertain the information required pursuant to paragraph (7) or (9) of subdivision (d) and to reduce that information to writing in accordance with the requirements of paragraph (1) once that information becomes known.

expectedJSON.gap: The statute does not define "material change," and it does not state a deadline for reducing newly known figures to writing beyond the requirement that the parties do so "once that information becomes known." The continuing duty described here is tied to the presumption in subdivision (b); the statute does not state a separate penalty for failing to update an estimate.

expectedJSON.body: A person or entity who enters into a contract or agreement referred to in subdivisions (d) or (e) must keep a copy of the written contract or agreement for not less than four years following the termination of the contract or agreement. On the Labor Commissioner's request, the person or entity must provide the Labor Commissioner a copy of the provisions of the contract or agreement, and any other documentation, related to paragraphs (1) to (10), inclusive, of subdivision (d). Documents obtained by the Labor Commissioner under this section are exempt from disclosure under the California Public Records Act.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, four-year retention and production to the Labor Commissioner
citations.quote: A person or entity who enters into a contract or agreement referred to in subdivisions (d) or (e) shall keep a copy of the written contract or agreement for a period of not less than four years following the termination of the contract or agreement. Upon the request of the Labor Commissioner, any person or entity who enters into the contract or agreement shall provide to the Labor Commissioner a copy of the provisions of the contract or agreement, and any other documentation, related to paragraphs (1) to (10), inclusive, of subdivision (d).

expectedJSON.gap: The retention duty attaches to contracts "referred to in subdivisions (d) or (e)" — that is, the written contracts and written material changes used to qualify for the presumption — and the statute does not state a separate penalty within Section 2810 for failing to retain or produce them. The Public Records Act exemption is stated by cross-reference to Division 10 (commencing with Section 7920.000) of Title 1 of the Government Code, whose terms are not set out in this section.

expectedJSON.body: An employee aggrieved by a violation of subdivision (a) may file an action for damages to recover the greater of all of the employee's actual damages or $250 per employee per violation for an initial violation and $1,000 per employee for each subsequent violation, and, on prevailing, may recover costs and reasonable attorney's fees. Such an action may not be maintained unless it is pleaded and proved that an employee was injured as a result of a violation of a labor law or regulation in connection with the performance of the contract or agreement. An aggrieved employee may also bring an action for injunctive relief and, on prevailing, may recover costs and reasonable attorney's fees.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, damages, penalties, costs, and fees
citations.quote: An employee aggrieved by a violation of subdivision (a) may file an action for damages to recover the greater of all of the employee’s actual damages or two hundred fifty dollars ($250) per employee per violation for an initial violation and one thousand dollars ($1,000) per employee for each subsequent violation, and, upon prevailing in an action brought pursuant to this section, may recover costs and reasonable attorney’s fees.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810(g)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, requirement to plead and prove injury
citations.quote: An action under this section shall not be maintained unless it is pleaded and proved that an employee was injured as a result of a violation of a labor law or regulation in connection with the performance of the contract or agreement.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810(g)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, injunctive relief
citations.quote: An employee aggrieved by a violation of subdivision (a) may also bring an action for injunctive relief and, upon prevailing, may recover costs and reasonable attorney’s fees.

expectedJSON.gap: The statute gives the private right of action to an "employee aggrieved by a violation of subdivision (a)" and does not, in this section, state a limitations period, address class treatment, or address enforcement by the Labor Commissioner through a citation. The injury requirement is a pleading-and-proof requirement tied to a violation of a labor law or regulation in connection with performance of the contract, which means a defective contract alone is not described by the statute as supporting a damages action.

expectedJSON.body: Section 2810 defines the knowledge element in three parts. The term "knows" includes knowledge, arising from familiarity with the normal facts and circumstances of the business activity engaged in, that the contract or agreement does not include funds sufficient to allow the contractor to comply with applicable laws. The phrase "should know" includes knowledge of any additional facts or information that would make a reasonably prudent person undertake to inquire whether, taken together, the contract or agreement contains sufficient funds to allow the contractor to comply with applicable laws. A failure by a person or entity to request or obtain any information from the contractor that is required by any applicable statute or by the contract between them constitutes knowledge of that information for purposes of the section. Construing these provisions, the Court of Appeal stated that they charge a contracting party with knowledge typical in the industry as well as with knowledge of any additional facts or information reasonably suggesting insufficiency, and that because subdivision (a) precludes entering into an insufficient contract, the party's knowledge is determined at the time the contract is executed.

citations.quote: The term “knows” includes the knowledge, arising from familiarity with the normal facts and circumstances of the business activity engaged in, that the contract or agreement does not include funds sufficient to allow the contractor to comply with applicable laws.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810(i)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, definition of "should know"
citations.quote: The phrase “should know” includes the knowledge of any additional facts or information that would make a reasonably prudent person undertake to inquire whether, taken together, the contract or agreement contains sufficient funds to allow the contractor to comply with applicable laws.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, failure to request required information
citations.quote: A failure by a person or entity to request or obtain any information from the contractor that is required by any applicable statute or by the contract or agreement between them, constitutes knowledge of that information for purposes of this section.

citations.quote: Taken together, these two provisions charge a contracting party with knowledge typical in the industry, as well as with knowledge of any “additional facts or information” reasonably suggesting insufficiency.

citations.cite: Court of Appeal on the time at which knowledge is measured
citations.quote: Because subdivision (a) precludes a contracting party from entering into an insufficient contract, the party’s knowledge must be determined at the time the contract is executed.

expectedJSON.gap: Each definition is phrased as what the term "includes," so the statutory text is not an exhaustive definition of actual or constructive knowledge. Castillo v. Toll Bros., Inc. is a decision of the First District Court of Appeal, and it construed the version of Section 2810 in effect before the 2024 amendment, when subdivision (a) reached a "construction, farm labor, garment, janitorial, or security guard contractor"; the knowledge definitions it construed appear at subdivision (i)(1) and (i)(2) in the current text as well. This sheet does not survey later decisions agreeing or disagreeing with Castillo.

expectedJSON.body: In Castillo v. Toll Bros., Inc., the First District Court of Appeal addressed wage-and-hour claims brought by subcontractors' employees against a homebuilder under Section 2810. The court described the determination called for by subdivision (a) as encompassing two separate questions for a complex contract: the contracting party's actual or constructive knowledge of insufficiency, which is prospective and evaluated when the contract is executed, and actual insufficiency, which is retrospective and can be determined only after the cost of performance is known. The court stated that a contracting party can be held liable under Section 2810 only if it knew or should have known the contract price was reasonably likely to be insufficient at the time the contract was executed and the contract price proved insufficient in practice. The court also rejected a narrower reading of "knows or should know" that would require genuine knowledge of insufficiency at signing, reasoning that such a definition would allow a contracting party to evade liability by cultivating ignorance in its contractual relations.

citations.quote: A contracting party can be held liable under section 2810 only if (1) it knew or should have known the contract price was reasonably likely to be insufficient at the time the contract was executed and (2) the contract price proved insufficient in practice.

citations.quote: The first question, the contracting party’s knowledge, is necessarily a prospective determination, evaluated at the time the contract was executed.

citations.quote: Only in unusual circumstances will the insufficiency of a contract be so clear that a contracting party can be said to have actual knowledge of the insufficiency, particularly if the contracting party has made no attempt to determine the details of the employer’s proposed performance.

expectedJSON.gap: Castillo is a Court of Appeal decision, not a decision of the California Supreme Court, and it arose on review of summary judgment and summary adjudication rulings; the court affirmed in part and reversed in part, remanding the Section 2810 claim in one of the two consolidated matters. The opinion construed an earlier version of the statute, quoting subdivision (a) as then reaching a "construction, farm labor, garment, janitorial, or security guard contractor," and its two-question framing is expressly addressed to a "complex contract" whose labor and materials costs cannot be known with certainty at signing. The sentence quoted here describing the two separate questions is quoted from "the determination called for" onward and ends before a footnote-reference marker that immediately follows the word "insufficiency" in the source text; the court's further statement that a narrow actual-knowledge rule "would defeat the obvious purpose of section 2810, since it would allow a contracting party to evade liability ... by cultivating ignorance in its contractual relations" is interrupted mid-sentence by a star-pagination marker (*1198) in the available text, so the adjacent unbroken sentences are quoted instead.

expectedJSON.body: Castillo v. Toll Bros., Inc. addressed which wage level is used to decide whether a contract includes sufficient funds. The plaintiffs argued that sufficiency should be measured against the locally prevailing wage for comparable work; the court held that the statutory language unambiguously requires the sufficiency of a contract challenged under Section 2810 to be measured by the minimum wage cost for the work anticipated. The court reasoned that there is no general law requiring an employer to pay its workers the average local wage for a particular skill or trade if that average wage is higher than the legal minimum, so paying less than the prevailing wage violates no law, and that Section 2810 imposes nothing more than compliance with legal requirements. The court used the term "minimum wage" to mean the minimum permissible wage under applicable state and local law for the work covered by the contract, noting that on some jobs, notably those requiring payment of the prevailing wage, the minimum permissible wage may be higher than the Industrial Welfare Commission's designated minimum wage.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause reports how one published Court of Appeal decision construed the statute; the statutory text itself refers only to "funds sufficient to allow the contractor to comply with all applicable local, state, and federal laws or regulations" and names no wage standard. The court's own footnote makes clear that where a prevailing wage law does apply to the work, the prevailing wage can be the minimum permissible wage, so the holding is about the absence of a free-floating market-wage requirement rather than about public works; the last two quotations below come from that footnote rather than from the body of the opinion. The first quotation begins mid-sentence, after the introductory words "Based on these provisions," in the source. Sufficiency also depends on costs beyond wages, such as legally required payroll contributions, which this clause does not enumerate, and Castillo construed the statute as it read before the 2024 amendment.
